samples.summary: `JWT_SECRET` accepted as a command-line argument (`--source-jwt-secret` / `--target-jwt-secret`), exposing the master signing key via the process table
samples.evidence: The new flags at packages/backend/scripts/copy-yorkie-documents.ts:83-90 take the deployment's `JWT_SECRET` as argv, and `usage()` (line 37) documents that invocation. Process arguments are world-readable on Linux (`ps aux`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`), are recorded in shell history, and are echoed by most CI runners. That value is the same secret `AuthService.createTokens` (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts:118-124) uses to sign session access tokens, and that `JwtStrategy` (packages/backend/src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts:24) verifies — so any local user or CI log reader who captures it can forge an `access` token for any `sub` and take over any account, and can also mint the unconditional `yorkie-service` token. The existing `--source-api-key` / `--database-url` flags set the precedent, but neither is the session-signing key. Prefer reading these from dedicated env vars (e.g. `SOURCE_JWT_SECRET`) or a file path.

samples.summary: Copy script silently signs the *target* side's auth token with the *source* deployment's `JWT_SECRET`, transmitting a source-signed credential to foreign infrastructure
samples.evidence: `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv(options.targetJwtSecret)` (line 238) falls back to `process.env.JWT_SECRET` when `--target-jwt-secret` is omitted (packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-service-token.ts:76). The CliOptions doc-comment at line 14-19 states the two sides are different deployments that "need not share a secret". So the default behaviour is: mint a token signed with YOUR production master secret and send it, over the network, to `--target-rpc-addr` — a Yorkie server operated by the other deployment, which will reject it anyway (its backend verifies with a different secret). The other side's operator (or anyone who can read that server's request logs) now holds a valid, unconditional `yorkie-service` token for YOUR deployment for its full TTL, granting read/write on every document via `decide()` (packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215), plus a signature sample of your JWT_SECRET. The target injector should default to nothing (anonymous) rather than to the source secret.

samples.summary: The new `yorkie-service` token is an unscoped, all-documents, all-methods bearer credential signed with the session secret, and the rationale justifying it ("never leaves the process") is factually wrong
samples.evidence: `decide()` returns ALLOW for `identity.typ === 'yorkie-service'` before any document key, verb, or method check, so one token authorizes PushPull, Watch, ListRevisions, GetRevision and RestoreRevision on every document in the deployment. Its payload (packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-service-token.ts:42) carries no `aud`, no document binding and no scope, its TTL is the operator-set `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN` (packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie.service.ts:52, can be hours or days), and it is signed with the same `JWT_SECRET` as user sessions. The justification comment at yorkie-service-token.ts:23-25 and controller.ts:212-213 says the token "never leaves the process" — it does, by design: `yorkie.Client({ authTokenInjector })` sends it to `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` (documented default `http://localhost:8080`, plaintext) on every RPC, and Yorkie echoes it verbatim in the auth-webhook body. Any capture point on that path (a proxy, an access log, a Yorkie server log, a non-TLS hop, a shared/hosted Yorkie) yields strictly more authority than any user token. Recommend binding it to the document key being attached, a distinct signing key, and a sub-minute TTL independent of `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN`.

samples.summary: `isYorkieAuthEnforced` disables enforcement on `FALSE` / `False` / ` false `, while the shipped operator docs promise only the exact literal `false` does
samples.evidence: `raw?.trim().toLowerCase() !== 'false'` accepts several spellings as the shadow-mode opt-out, and the controller spec pins `'FALSE'` and `' false '` as non-enforcing (packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.spec.ts:313-314). packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:185 tells operators to "Set it to `false` — and only that exact value", and packages/backend/README.md:101 says "The literal `false`, and only that". The code is more permissive than documented in the one direction that turns access control OFF: a Helm/Python/Terraform-rendered boolean emits `False`, which silently selects shadow mode where the docs say it would enforce. Either match the docs (exact `=== 'false'`) or correct both docs.

samples.summary: Several security-relevant docs still tell operators enforcement is off by default, contradicting the new default and inviting an explicit `=false`
samples.evidence: This change flips the default to enforce but leaves at least these saying the opposite: docs/design/sharing.md:208 ("This is **off by default**. `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE` is unset in a stock deployment, which puts the controller in shadow mode") and :233, docs/design/revision-history.md:504, docs/design/template-gallery.md:668, docs/design/docs/docs-image-editing.md:301, packages/frontend/README.md:37, packages/docs/src/store/read-only.ts:40 and packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:4413. An operator following sharing.md concludes the client-side read-only gates are the write boundary, and one following the old rollout wording sets `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=false` explicitly — which under the new reading is the only value that disables per-document access control, permanently leaving a share-link viewer able to write.

samples.summary: No regression test pins that a `yorkie-service` token cannot be replayed as a Bearer session or accepted where a user identity is expected
samples.evidence: `verifyYorkieToken` now accepts a third `typ` (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts:99-105) whose payload has no `sub`. I traced the replay path and it is safe today — `JwtStrategy.validate` requires `payload.tokenType === 'access'` (packages/backend/src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts:36) and the service payload has no `tokenType` — but the existing replay tests (auth.service.spec.ts:87, :103, jwt.strategy.spec.ts) only cover the `yorkie` and access/refresh shapes. A future subject-less consumer of `YorkieTokenPayload` that reads `payload.sub` would get `undefined` with no test objecting. Add a case asserting the service token is rejected by `JwtStrategy` and that no `hasAccess` path can be reached with it.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as claimed. copy-yorkie-documents.ts:83-90 assigns `--source-jwt-secret`/`--target-jwt-secret` directly from argv, and usage() at :37 and :40-42 documents that invocation, explicitly naming the value as the deployment's JWT_SECRET. Those values flow at :232-240 into yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv (yorkie-service-token.ts:75-87), whose parameter defaults to process.env.JWT_SECRET and is used at :38-46 to sign the subject-less, unconditional `yorkie-service` token. That same secret signs and verifies user session access tokens (auth.service.ts:58 `requireConfig('JWT_SECRET')`; jwt.strategy.ts:24 `secretOrKey: configService.get('JWT_SECRET')`), so a local user reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, shell history, or a CI command echo obtains the master signing key and can forge an access token for any `sub`. No refutation ground holds: the code is present (not `not-present`); the env-var default in yorkie-service-token.ts:76 is only a fallback and imposes no guard on the argv path, which parseArgs accepts silently and usage() advertises (not `already-guarded`); and secrets exposure / sensitive-data disclosure is explicitly inside this lens's lane with high impact-if-real, so I cannot call it `out-of-scope`.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. copy-yorkie-documents.ts:236-241 builds the TARGET Yorkie client with `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv(options.targetJwtSecret)`, and `--target-jwt-secret` is optional (parsed at :87-90, not in the required-arg check at :112-121). yorkie-service-token.ts:75-77 defaults that parameter to `process.env.JWT_SECRET`, so the default behaviour is to mint a token signed with the SOURCE deployment's master secret and transmit it to the operator-supplied `--target-rpc-addr`, which forwards it to that deployment's auth webhook/logs. The script's own CliOptions comment (:14-19) and usage text (:40-42) state the two sides are different deployments that need not share a secret, so the leaking configuration is the documented default. Impact is real: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217 allows any `typ === 'yorkie-service'` token unconditionally — no document, verb, or subject check — so a captured token grants read/write on every document of the source deployment for its TTL (default 10m, yorkie-service-token.ts:77). This directly breaks the invariant asserted in that controller's comment at :212-213 ("the token ... never leaves the process, so nothing outside this server can present one"). I enumerated all four call sites of yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv (copy-yorkie-documents.ts:232,238; migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347; migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221) and found no guard tying the signing secret to the destination endpoint. The only mitigation is that the documented invocation (docs/tasks/archive/2026/03/20260314-local-prod-restore-todo.md:77) uses localhost on both sides and the script is operator-run — that lowers likelihood but not impact, and gives no named refutation ground. Credential exposure to foreign infrastructure is in the Security lane.

verdict.reason: All claimed code is present as described. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217 returns the blanket ALLOW for identity.typ === 'yorkie-service' before the CLIENT_METHODS check (:220), the attributes-presence fail-closed check (:228), and checkAttribute/hasAccess (:236-241) — so one token authorizes every method, including the privileged REVISION_READ_METHODS (:83, :257), on every document key. The payload is literally only { typ: 'yorkie-service' } (yorkie-service-token.ts:42): no aud, no document binding, no scope. It is signed and verified with accessSecret = requireConfig('JWT_SECRET') (auth.service.ts:58, :97), the same key as user access tokens (:118-121), with TTL from the operator-set YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN (yorkie.service.ts:52-55). The justifying comment ("never leaves the process", yorkie-service-token.ts:23-25 and controller.ts:212-213) is refuted by the code itself: the injector is handed to new yorkie.Client({ rpcAddr, apiKey, authTokenInjector }) (yorkie.service.ts:70-74) and sent to YORKIE_RPC_ADDR, default plaintext http://localhost:8080 (yorkie.service.ts:40-42), and Yorkie echoes it verbatim in the webhook body (auth.service.ts:32-33). No guard mitigates this: YorkieSignatureGuard only proves the caller is Yorkie, and shadow mode (:168) only widens access. Since the Yorkie project public key ships in every visitor's bundle (controller.ts:96-105), a token captured on that path grants read/write on all documents — strictly more authority than any user token. In-lane (over-broad authorization gate plus bearer-secret exposure) and correctly rated major.
